title: The Building That Doesn't Exist
setting: a small radio station's call-in line

post.author: u/dead_air_dana
post.title: I screen calls for a tiny late-night radio show. At 2:13 AM a woman called to tell us we don't exist.

blocks.text: I produce *The Graveyard Line* on Hollow Pine 97.3, a station so small our studio used to be a dentist's office. One to four AM, I screen the calls. Truckers, nurses, insomniacs, and one man who only wants to talk about owls.

On Tuesday at 4 PM, Marcus, our volunteer computer guy, moved our website to a new machine. Its only job is to hand our site to anyone who asks for it. A computer like that is called a server. The old one had hummed in the studio closet for ten years. Marcus changed the address listed under our website's name, hollowpinefm.com. He watched the site load from the new machine on his phone, and switched the old one off. "Nobody will notice," he said.
At 2:13 AM a woman named Ivy called. She lives four streets from the studio.
"I listen through your website," she said. "Tonight it says you're not there. Not broken. Not there. *This site can't be reached.* Like nothing lives at that address anymore."
Our site was open on the studio computer while she said it. The show playing live through it. Song list updating.
I started asking every caller. Seven could see us. Two couldn't: Ivy, and a night nurse across town. Different streets, same internet company. Bramblewire.

The owl man used to fix phone lines. "Computers don't find each other by name," he said. "They find each other by number, like phones do. Every website lives at a number, called its IP address. IP is short for internet protocol, the rules computers use to talk. Something has to turn the name you type into that number. That's DNS, short for domain name system. Think of it as the internet's phone book."

"And nobody reads the phone book themselves," he said. "Your internet company keeps a helper that looks names up for you and remembers the answers for a while. That helper is called a resolver. It checks its saved answers. If none, it asks the phone book, keeps the answer, and tells you." He had me read Ivy a command letter by letter: a line she typed to ask her resolver for our address directly, without the web browser in between. Then I typed the same command on the studio computer. Each line it printed shows the time, whose computer asked, our name, a number I didn't understand yet, an A for address, and the address that came back.

02:21:00  ivy's laptop  hollowpinefm.com  44760  A  203.0.113.7
02:21:00  studio pc     hollowpinefm.com  83120  A  198.51.100.24
02:22:00  ivy's laptop  hollowpinefm.com  44700  A  203.0.113.7
Same name. Same minute. Two different addresses. Marcus texted back at 3 AM: 203.0.113.7 is the old server. The one in the closet. The one with no power.
And the number after our name on Ivy's lines kept shrinking. Sixty every minute. One every second. At 3:58 AM I had her run it one last time: 38940. It never once went up.
Her internet still sends her to the building we moved out of.

Ivy says she'll try again tonight. Next month Marcus moves our stream server, the computer that sends out our live audio. What happens when that number hits zero? And how do we make sure nobody else gets sent to an empty building?

blocks.label: two_lookups.png

diagram.aria: Two lookups of hollowpinefm.com at 2:21 AM. Ivy's laptop asks Bramblewire's resolver, which answers 203.0.113.7 from its cache with 44,760 seconds left, so Ivy connects to the old server, which is switched off and never answers. The studio PC asks the studio's resolver, which asked after the move and answers 198.51.100.24, so the studio reaches the new server and the show plays.

blocks.caption: I drew this after the show. Same name, same minute, two answers. Bramblewire's resolver is still handing out the old address from its saved copy, its cache, with 44,760 seconds left on the clock.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: That number after your name on her lines is a countdown in seconds. Your name's entry in the phone book, the line saying which number it points to, is called a DNS record. Each record carries a timer: how long a resolver may keep its saved copy before it must ask again. That timer is the TTL, short for time to live. It works in steps. First the resolver looks the name up and saves the answer with the timer. Then the timer counts down one every second while it hands that saved answer to everyone. When it hits zero, the copy is thrown away, and the next person to ask makes the resolver look the name up again. Divide the number by 3600 to get hours, and add that to 2:21 AM. Then ask Marcus what the TTL on that record was before he moved anything.

replies.author: u/dead_air_dana
replies.text: 12.43 hours. So 2:47 this afternoon? Marcus says he never touched the TTL. He didn't know the record had one.

comments.author: u/insomniac_ruth
comments.text: I'm on Bramblewire too. Couldn't see you either. Cleared my browser's saved copies of sites. Unplugged the router, the box my internet comes in through, and plugged it back in. Nothing. Then I took my phone off the home internet and onto mobile data, the phone company's own internet. And there you were. Same phone. Same room.

comments.author: u/packet_ghost
comments.text: Everyone's going to tell you to clear your cache. A cache is just a pile of saved answers, kept so nobody has to ask twice, like a note of a number you looked up once. Ask yourself *whose* cache. Her laptop keeps one. So does her internet company's resolver. A visit usually goes in order: first her laptop checks its own saved answers; if it has none, it asks the resolver; the resolver checks its own, and only asks the phone book if it has none either. Clearing her laptop only empties the first stop. On mobile data, a different company's resolver answers, and that one had the new address.

reply.prompt: Marcus moves the stream server next month. What should he do so nobody gets sent to an empty building again? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Tell listeners to clear their browser's saved answers and restart their internet box after every move.
options.part2: We read a notice on air every hour: clear your browser's saved copies, restart your internet box. Ivy did all of it, twice. She left her box unplugged until morning. When she plugged it back in, the page still said we weren't there. Nothing in her house was holding the old address. Something outside it was.
options.senior: Clearing your own saved copies only helps if your resolver already has the new answer. Bramblewire's resolver held the old one for a full day, and no listener can reach into it.

options.text: Set the TTL to 60 seconds and keep it there for good, so every change shows up within a minute.
options.part2: Marcus set the TTL to 60 seconds and left it there. The stream move went smoothly, and most listeners followed us within a minute or two. But the company that runs our phone-book entry charges for every question, and our bill crept up. First visits felt a hair slower. And one listener's internet company kept the old address for an hour anyway, because its resolver never keeps anything for less than an hour.
options.senior: A short TTL makes changes show up fast. But every resolver has to come back and ask far more often. That means more traffic, a bigger bill if your DNS company charges per question, and a slightly slower first visit. Some resolvers also set their own minimum time and ignore yours. Go short around a change, then raise it.

options.text: A day ahead, cut the TTL to 5 minutes; after the move, keep the old server on until visits stop.
options.part2: Two days before the move, Marcus lowered our TTL to 5 minutes. We waited out the old day-long copies, moved the stream on Thursday at 4 PM, and left the old server running. By 4:10, Ivy could hear us. So could everyone on Bramblewire. Visits to the old server dropped to almost nothing within the hour. Almost. Every night since, at 2:13 AM, something knocks on the old server and asks for the stream. It never looks up our name first. It already knows where we used to live.
options.senior: Lower the TTL early: at least as long before the move as the old TTL was. Keep the old address answering until visits to it die out, then raise the TTL again. You can't clear the world's saved copies, but you can decide how long they keep you.

options.text: After the move, phone Bramblewire and ask them to wipe the saved answers on their resolver.
options.part2: I called Bramblewire at 9 AM. After 40 minutes on hold, a tired man wiped their resolver's saved answers, and Ivy could hear us by lunch. Next month we moved the stream. This time it was Bramblewire, a phone company two towns over, and a college network I'd never heard of. I can't call every company on Earth. I tried.
options.senior: You can't clear saved copies you don't control, and there are resolvers everywhere: internet companies, offices, phone companies and free public ones anyone can use. The one thing you control is the TTL on your own record, and it only helps if you change it before the move.

sim.title: Look up the station yourself
sim.lede: You're Ivy. Each dot is one visit to hollowpinefm.com. The clock runs 600 times faster than real life, so an hour passes in 6 seconds. The dots move in slow motion: in real life, finding an address takes milliseconds. Click any box to see what it does.
sim.tryThis: Try this: visit twice and watch the second visit come straight from your laptop's cache, without asking anyone. Press Move, then visit: the dead server. Flush (clear) your own cache and visit again: still dead, because the resolver's copy is still counting down. Then reset, set the TTL to 5 minutes before your first visit, move, wait a moment, and visit.

explain.oneLine: Nothing vanished. Ivy's internet company kept handing out the station's old address, because the station's phone-book entry had told it to keep that answer for a whole day.

steps.title: Computers find each other by number.
steps.text: Every machine on the internet has a number, like 198.51.100.24. Think of it as a street address. It is called an IP address (IP is short for internet protocol). People remember names like hollowpinefm.com instead, so something has to turn the name into the number. That something is DNS, short for domain name system: the internet's phone book.

steps.title: Ivy's internet company does the looking up for her.
steps.text: Ivy's laptop doesn't search the phone book itself. First it checks its own saved answers. If it has none, it asks a resolver, a lookup helper run by her internet company, Bramblewire. The resolver checks its own saved answers next. If it has a fresh one, it hands it straight back without asking anyone, even if the record has changed since. If it has no fresh answer saved, it asks around, like a caller passed from desk to desk. First a root server, the top of the phone book, points it to the servers that look after .com names. The ending of a name, like .com, is its TLD, short for top-level domain. One of those .com servers points it to the station's own nameserver, the server that holds the station's entries. That nameserver answers with the station's A record: the entry that gives the address. If that nameserver can't be reached, the lookup usually fails, and the site seems not to exist. Otherwise the resolver saves the answer, hands it to Ivy's laptop, and her browser connects to that address. The resolver saves those pointers too, usually for about two days. So when only its copy of the address has run out, it normally goes straight back to the station's nameserver.

steps.title: Every answer comes with a timer.
steps.text: The record also carries a TTL, short for time to live. It says how many seconds anyone may keep a copy before asking again. The station's was 86400 seconds, one day. On Tuesday at 2:47 PM, Bramblewire's resolver looked up the station. It saved 203.0.113.7 until 2:47 PM Wednesday. Ivy's laptop keeps a copy of its own too, counting down the same timer. Each second, the timer drops by one. Until it reaches zero, every question gets the saved copy, even if the record has changed. At zero, the copy is thrown away. The next question makes the resolver look the name up again and start a new timer.

steps.title: Marcus changed the record at 4 PM. The copies never heard.
steps.text: Within about a minute, the station's nameserver was answering 198.51.100.24. But a resolver doesn't ask again until its timer runs out. So Bramblewire kept sending Ivy, the night nurse and every other customer to the old server, which was switched off. The number in her lines was that timer: 44,760 seconds at 2:21 AM is 12 hours and 26 minutes, which lands on 2:47 PM. The studio's resolver had last asked at 1:26 AM, after the move. So its line showed the new address, with 83,120 seconds left.

steps.title: "Propagation" is mostly saved copies expiring.
steps.text: People say a DNS change needs time to propagate, to spread, as if it travels. A record change barely travels. Within about a minute it is live on the domain's own nameservers. Route 53, Amazon's DNS service, says changes generally reach all of its nameservers within 60 seconds. Some domains also have backup nameservers at other companies, called secondary nameservers. They usually catch up soon after: the main one sends them a short alert called a NOTIFY message, and they fetch a fresh copy of the records, called a zone transfer. The real wait is every cache in the world, every saved copy, letting its old copy expire, each on its own timer. The longest wait is the old TTL. The famous "24 to 48 hours" mostly comes from a different change: moving a domain to new nameservers. For a .com name, the .com servers hand out its NS record, the list of its nameservers. That record has a TTL of 172800 seconds, two days. It is set by the registry, the organization that runs .com, not by the owner. Marcus only changed an A record with a one-day TTL, which is why Ivy will hear the show again tonight.

diagram.aria: The lookup path. 1: Ivy's browser asks Bramblewire's resolver where hollowpinefm.com is. On a cache miss the resolver asks, in order, 2: a root server, 3: a .com TLD server and 4: the station's nameserver, whose A record now says 198.51.100.24 with a TTL of 86400 seconds. Bramblewire's cache still holds 203.0.113.7 until Wednesday 2:47 PM, so 5: Ivy connects to the old server, which is switched off. Everyone else lands on the new server.

explain.caption: Each arrow is a question, and each one gets an answer back. Steps 2 to 4 happen only on a cache miss, when the resolver has no fresh copy saved. A resolver that still has the root's and .com's pointers saved (they usually last about two days) skips straight to step 4. Bramblewire's resolver asked on Tuesday at 2:47 PM, got 203.0.113.7 with a one-day TTL, and won't ask again until 2:47 PM Wednesday. The record changed at 4 PM, but step 5 still sends Ivy to the old server.

fix.title: The fix: lower the TTL before the move, raise it after
fix.text: Engineers call a move like Marcus's a migration, and the DNS part has a standard routine. A day or more before the move (at least as long as the current TTL), lower the record's TTL to something short, such as 300 seconds. Then wait for the old one-day copies to expire everywhere. If you skip this wait, any copy saved just before you lowered the TTL still lasts the old full day. On moving day, every cache that obeys the timer holds your address for 5 minutes at most. Move, and keep the old server answering for a few days. It can serve the site itself or pass visitors on to the new one. Either way, anyone still holding the old address gets the show instead of silence. When visits to the old server have stopped and the new one is solid, raise the TTL back to an hour or a day.

limits: Not every cache obeys the timer. Some resolvers set their own shortest or longest keeping time. Some keep using an expired answer when they can't reach your nameserver, a standard feature called serve-stale: the copy runs out, the resolver tries to ask again, no answer comes, so it hands out the old copy instead. And some programs can be set to keep an address forever. That's why the old server stays up for a while.

You can't clear (flush) saved copies you don't control. Clearing your own browser's or OS's copies (OS is short for operating system, the core software of your laptop or phone) only helps if your resolver already has the new answer. Only Bramblewire could clear Bramblewire's resolver.

A short TTL costs something. Resolvers ask your nameserver far more often. That means more queries (single questions), a bigger bill on paid DNS services, and a slightly slower first visit each time a copy expires. That's why you raise it again after the move.

head: TTL on your record
Good
Bad
rows: Changes reach almost everyone within minutes. A bad change is quick to undo.
Many more questions to your nameserver. Slightly slower first visits. A bigger bill on paid DNS.
Fewer questions, faster repeat visits, cheaper. Saved copies keep working if your nameserver stops answering for a short while.
A move or a mistake can take a full TTL to clear, and you can't speed it up afterwards.
Fast when it matters, cheap the rest of the time.
Takes planning: you have to remember a day before the move.

explain.seniorTake: A record change reaches your own nameservers within a minute. The real wait is old saved answers expiring. So the deadline for a move is set a day earlier, by the TTL you chose long ago. Lower it before you need it, and keep the old building open until the last visitor has left.

realWorld.title: Facebook, October 4, 2021
realWorld.text: Facebook's problem was the opposite of Ivy's: the phone book itself became unreachable. Facebook keeps its servers in data centers, buildings full of computers, linked by its own private network, called a backbone. During routine maintenance, a command meant to check how much that backbone could carry accidentally took every one of its links down. A safety tool that should have stopped the command had a bug. Facebook's DNS servers are built to take themselves offline when they can't reach the data centers, because that usually means the network is unhealthy. So they did. They stopped announcing their routes over BGP, short for Border Gateway Protocol: the system networks use to tell each other which addresses they can reach. The nameservers were still running, but nobody could reach them. So the rest of the internet could no longer find Facebook's servers. To the world, facebook.com was a building that didn't exist.

realWorld.title: What resolvers saw that day
realWorld.text: Cloudflare runs 1.1.1.1, a free public resolver anyone can use. On it, lookups for facebook.com started failing at around 15:50 UTC (UTC is the world clock engineers share) and worked again at 21:20 UTC, about five and a half hours later. Apps and people kept trying again, so Cloudflare's resolvers worldwide handled about 30 times more questions than usual. A name that can't be looked up is a site that can't be reached, even when the servers are healthy.

realWorld.title: AWS Route 53's own advice
realWorld.text: Route 53, Amazon's DNS service, describes the same trade-off in its documentation. A longer TTL means resolvers ask less often. That makes lookups faster and lowers your Route 53 bill. But a change, such as a new IP address, takes longer to take effect. For a name that's already in use, it recommends setting a shorter value first, such as 300 seconds. Then raise it after you confirm the new settings are correct.

asked: What happens when you type a URL and press Enter?
You're moving a website to a new server. How do you keep it reachable while DNS catches up?
interview.answer: Walk the lookup in order. First the browser's saved copies, then the operating system's, then the resolver. If the resolver has nothing fresh, it asks a root server, then a TLD server (the one for the name's ending, like .com), then the authoritative nameserver, the one holding the owner's official records. It skips the first two when it still has their pointers saved. It then keeps the A record for its TTL. Then the move: lower the TTL ahead of time, by at least as long as the old TTL, and wait. Switch, keep the old server answering until visits to it die out, then raise the TTL. Name the limits before they ask: saved copies you don't control, programs that ignore TTLs, the extra questions a short TTL brings, and the two-day wait a nameserver change still carries at .com.

terms.def: The number of a machine on the internet, like 198.51.100.24. It works like a street address: to reach a machine, you need its number. IP is short for internet protocol.
The human-friendly name of a website, like hollowpinefm.com. People remember names and machines need numbers, so something has to translate.
The full web address you type, like https://hollowpinefm.com/schedule. The domain name is the part in the middle.
A computer that waits for requests and answers them. A web server sends you a site's pages. A nameserver answers DNS questions.
The app you use to visit websites, such as Chrome, Firefox or Safari. It keeps a few recent DNS answers saved, like notes by the phone.
The core software that runs a computer or phone, like Windows, macOS or Android. It keeps its own saved DNS answers, shared by every app on the machine.
Short for operating system. The OS's saved DNS answers are shared by every app on your laptop or phone.
Internet service provider: the company that connects your home or phone to the internet, like Bramblewire in this story. Most run a resolver for their customers.
The box in your home that your internet comes in through. It connects your devices to your internet company.
Domain name system: the internet's phone book. Servers around the world that turn names like hollowpinefm.com into IP addresses.
The helper that looks names up for you, usually run by your internet company. It answers from its saved copies, or asks around and then hands back the address.
A free resolver anyone can use instead of their internet company's, such as Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 or Google's 8.8.8.8.
A server that holds part of the phone book and answers questions about it. Root servers, TLD servers and authoritative nameservers are all nameservers.
The first stop in a full lookup. It doesn't know any website's address. It only knows which servers look after each ending, like .com or .org.
Top-level domain: the ending of a name, like .com or .org. A TLD server knows which nameserver holds the entries for each name with that ending.
The organization that runs an ending like .com and its servers. It usually sets the TTL on the NS records those servers hand out.
The nameserver that holds a domain's official records, set by its owner. Every other answer out there is a saved copy of what it said.
An extra nameserver, often run by another company, that keeps a copy of a domain's records and answers too, so the domain still works if the main one fails.
A DNS message a domain's main nameserver sends to its secondary nameservers when the records change, so they fetch the new version right away instead of waiting.
How a secondary nameserver fetches a fresh copy of a domain's records from the main nameserver.
One entry in a domain's DNS settings, such as which IP address the name points to. Each record has a type, a value and a TTL.
The DNS record that links a name to an IP address. A stands for address. The A in the station's lookup lines means this kind of record.
The DNS record that lists a domain's nameservers. The .com servers hold one for every .com name, which is how they point resolvers to the right nameserver.
Time to live: a number of seconds attached to every DNS answer, saying how long anyone may keep a copy before asking again. 86400 seconds is one day.
Saved copies of answers, kept so you don't have to ask again, like a number jotted by the phone. Fast, but it can go stale: it keeps the old answer until it expires.
Saved DNS answers. Your browser, your operating system and your resolver each keep their own, and each copy expires on its own TTL timer.
When a fresh answer is already saved in a cache, so nobody else has to be asked.
When a cache has no fresh answer, so the question has to go further. For a resolver, that means a full lookup.
Finding the IP address for a name, like "what is the address of hollowpinefm.com?" It may be answered from a cache or by asking around.
One question sent to a DNS server. A full lookup takes several: one to a root server, one to a TLD server, one to the authoritative nameserver.
What a resolver does on a cache miss: it asks a root server, then a TLD server, then the authoritative nameserver, and saves the answer for its TTL.
To clear a cache on purpose, so the next request has to ask again. You can only flush caches you control.

What people call the wait after a DNS change. A record change reaches your own nameservers within about a minute. The wait after that is old cached copies expiring, up to two days for a .com nameserver change.
Moving a system from one place to another, like a website from an old server to a new one.
Audio or video sent over the internet as it happens, so listeners can hear the show live in a browser.
A building full of servers, with its own power, cooling and network links.
A company's own high-speed network linking its data centers to each other and to the rest of the internet.
Border Gateway Protocol: how networks tell each other which IP addresses they can reach, like road signs. If a network stops announcing a route, nobody can find the way there.
A standard resolver feature: when the owner's nameserver can't be reached, the resolver keeps handing out its expired copy instead of giving no answer.
Coordinated Universal Time, the clock engineers use so timestamps from around the world line up.
Amazon Web Services, Amazon's cloud. Companies rent servers, storage and services like Route 53 from it.
Amazon's DNS service, part of AWS. It runs authoritative nameservers for your domains and lets you edit their records and TTLs.
In Route 53, the container that holds one domain's DNS records.
A Route 53 record that points a name straight at an Amazon service, such as a load balancer or CloudFront. You can't set its TTL: Route 53 uses the service's own default.
Application Load Balancer: an AWS service that takes a website's incoming visitors and shares them out across several servers, like a host seating diners.
Amazon's content delivery network: servers around the world that keep copies of a site's files close to visitors, so pages load faster.

atWork: Open Route 53 in your AWS account (AWS is Amazon Web Services, Amazon's rented computers and services), or ask whoever runs your DNS. Pick a record your team depends on, such as the A record for your main website. Read its TTL. Many Route 53 records that point a website at an ALB (a load balancer, which shares visitors across servers) or CloudFront (Amazon's worldwide copies of a site) are alias records. Those have no TTL you can set, because Route 53 uses the target's default. If yours is one, pick a record that shows a TTL. Work out how long a bad change to that record could keep sending users to the wrong place. Then write down three things: what you would set it to a day before moving that server (300 seconds is a common choice), how long you would wait before the move, and who will raise it again afterwards. If you can only look, not change, the hosted zone (Route 53's folder of one domain's records) lists every TTL.

recall.prompt: Ivy kept getting the old address for hours after the station changed its record. What decided how long?
options: The TTL on the station's DNS record
How far Ivy lives from the station
How busy the root servers were
recall.why: The TTL, the record's keep-it-for timer, tells every resolver how long it may keep a copy. The station's was one day, so Bramblewire's resolver kept the old answer for up to a day after it last asked.

recall.prompt: It's Wednesday. Your team moves the company website to a new server on Friday at 6 PM. The A record, the entry giving the site's address, has a TTL of 86400 seconds. What do you do, and when?

keyIdeas.idea: Lower the TTL now, well before Friday
The old one-day copies must expire before the move
Keep the old server running after the move, then raise the TTL again

recall.model: Lower the TTL today, to around 300 seconds. Resolvers that already saved the record keep their one-day copy. So lowering it on Wednesday means every old copy has expired by Thursday evening, well before Friday's move. After the switch, the worst case is about 5 minutes of old answers. Keep the old server running for a few days, for resolvers and programs that ignore the TTL, and watch its visits fall. Once the new server is solid, raise the TTL back to an hour or a day.

recall.prompt: Your internet provider's resolver still has an old address for a site. Which of these actually gets you to the new server?
options: Waiting for the resolver's copy to expire, or using a different resolver
Reloading the page over and over
recall.why: Your own saved copies aren't the problem: the resolver hands the old answer right back. Only its timer running out, or asking a different resolver (like a phone on mobile data), gets a fresh answer.

recall.prompt: A resolver has nothing saved at all. In what order does it ask?
options: .com TLD server, then root server, then the station's nameserver
The station's nameserver, then the root server
The old server, then the new server
Root server, then .com TLD server, then the station's nameserver
recall.why: Each step points to the next. The root knows who runs .com. The .com servers know which nameserver holds the station's records. And that nameserver, the one with the owner's official records, has the answer. Once those pointers are saved, later lookups usually go straight to the station's nameserver.

recall.prompt: A coworker says: "DNS changes take 24 to 48 hours to propagate, nothing we can do." What is actually happening, and what could they have done?

keyIdeas.idea: Very little travels: cached copies are expiring
The wait is set by the TTL
Lowering the TTL ahead of time shortens the wait

recall.model: Very little is travelling. A record change reaches the domain's own nameservers within about a minute. What takes time is resolvers and devices around the world holding old copies until each copy's TTL runs out. So the wait is set by the TTL the record had before the change. If they had lowered it to a few minutes a day or two ahead, most of the world would have switched within minutes. The one place 24 to 48 hours is real is a nameserver change. The .com servers hand out a domain's NS record, its list of nameservers, with a two-day TTL that the owner can't lower. So keep the old DNS service answering correctly for at least two days after the switch.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. Marcus is moving our show archive, every old episode, to a new server this Thursday at 4 PM. The archive has its own name, archive.hollowpinefm.com, with a TTL of 86400. It's Monday night. His plan: lower the TTL to 60 seconds on Thursday morning, "to be safe," move at 4, and switch the old server off at 4:05. Ivy already asked if she should be worried.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to the person who wrote the post. Is Marcus's plan okay? What should the timeline be?

keyIdeas.idea: Thursday morning is too late: copies saved before then keep their one-day timer
Lower it now, at least a day before the move
Don't switch the old server off right away

coldCase.model: Thursday morning is too late. A resolver that fetched the old record at 8 AM Thursday got a one-day timer. It keeps that copy until 8 AM Friday, long after the 4 PM move. Lower the TTL tonight, so every one-day copy has expired by Tuesday night. Then Thursday's move reaches nearly everyone within a minute. And don't switch the old server off at 4:05. Keep it serving for a few days, for resolvers and programs that ignore the TTL. Watch its visits drop to zero, then turn it off and raise the TTL again.
